design_detail: Single-author narrative review published as an Addiction 'Monograph' (online-first PDF, © 2014, pages numbered 1–17; 165 references), presented at the 'Through the Maze: Cannabis and Health' international drug-policy symposium in Auckland in November 2013. For each adverse health effect it summarizes what the author's 1993 review for the Australian government concluded (Hall, Solowij & Lemon, 1994), why, and what can reasonably be inferred in 2013. No search strategy, selection criteria, appraisal tool or pooling; the abstract's Methods is a comparison of the 1993 evidence with that of 2013. It restates the 1993 approach: four causal criteria (an association in case–control and prospective studies; reverse causation implausible; confounding controlled in prospective studies; biological plausibility), a standard of proof of 'more likely than not', inference by analogy with tobacco smoking (respiratory disease), alcohol (driving) and long-acting CNS depressants, and the same evidential standards as for alcohol and tobacco. It ends with bullet conclusions and Table 1, which rates 14 outcomes by evidence (+++, ++, +?), level of evidence and strength of effect.
can_establish: How the author of the 1993 Australian review judged in 2013 that the evidence on the adverse effects of recreational cannabis had changed, the causal criteria and standard of proof he applied, and which primary studies and figures he relied on for each conclusion (useful as a map to the primary literature up to 2013).
cannot_establish: Any effect size as first-hand evidence: every figure is second-hand, several have no citation and one absolute-risk estimate is the author's own calculation. Nor can it show that the evidence summarized is complete (no search method), that the associations it lists are causal (the body reports that the common-cause explanation of the psychosis association is hard to exclude and that a discordant-twin analysis removed the school-leaving association), or anything about sleep (beyond insomnia listed as a withdrawal symptom), edibles, vaping or cannabinoid hyperemesis, which it does not discuss. Its Table 1 ratings are not a defined grading system.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). No search method is reported; the acknowledgements thank an assistant for help with literature searches (pp. 12–13). The evidence is organized against the author's own 1993 review (ref 9).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; studies chosen by the author.
sample.demographics: Not applicable. The cited studies come mainly from the USA, Australia, New Zealand and Europe (Sweden, the Netherlands, Germany, the UK, France, Switzerland, Norway).
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the author's. 13 of 165 references have the author as a co-author (refs 2, 6, 9, 11, 41, 49, 51, 70, 84, 98, 107, 157, 163) and three more are chapters in a book he co-edited (refs 14, 134, 139). The 13 take 31 of 225 citation instances in the text (editors' count from the text extraction); the author's book with Pacula (2010, ref 6) and his 1994 review (ref 9) are the two most-cited sources (10 and 6 instances). The framework, the list of outcomes and the 1993 conclusions compared are the author's own. The review covers harms only, by design.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. The review states that epidemiological studies usually cannot measure the doses of THC and other cannabinoids that people receive, so heavy or regular use is defined as daily or near-daily use (p. 4), and that it deals mainly with regular, typically daily, cannabis smoking (p. 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Exposures differ between the cited estimates and must be carried with each figure: recent use shown by blood THC or self-report (crash meta-analysis); ever use, and the category the review calls regular use (pooled psychosis odds ratios); cannabis tried by 18, and ten or more uses by 18 (Swedish conscripts); 50 or more uses by 18, as the review puts it (lung cancer); early-onset, persistent near-daily use into the late 30s (Dunedin IQ); first use before 15 and earlier age at first use (school leaving); heaviest use at 18 (depression); more than weekly use (suicidal ideation; testicular cancer); heavy use (Rasic et al., 2013); treatment for a cannabis use disorder (Norwegian suicide study); five or more joints a day for 10 or more years (one MRI study); a median of three to five joints a month described as low levels (CARDIA). Route: smoking throughout; tobacco co-use and mixing tobacco into joints are discussed (pp. 7, 10). Potency: US THC content from under 2% in 1980 to 8.5% in 2006 (p. 1).
exposure.polysubstance: Treated as the main confounder: people who use cannabis regularly are more likely to use alcohol, tobacco and other illicit drugs and differ in risk-taking (p. 4); most people who smoke cannabis have smoked or still smoke tobacco, which leaves respiratory and cancer effects unclear (abstract, p. 1; pp. 9–10); 91% of the heaviest Swedish conscripts also smoked tobacco (p. 10); many in the Norwegian treatment cohort had injected drugs (p. 9). Statistical adjustment, fixed-effects regression and discordant-twin designs are described as the ways confounding has been tested (pp. 4, 7).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: For cognition, as cited: partial recovery after 2 years of abstinence (Solowij, 2002; Solowij & Pesa, 2012); persistent dose-related impairment after 28 days (Bolla et al., 2002); full recovery after 28 days (Pope et al., 2001); in Dunedin, some recovery after a year or more without use, and no decline in people who started as adults and had not used for a year or more before follow-up (pp. 5–6). Functional imaging after 28 days of abstinence (Block et al., 2002); CB1 receptor down-regulation lasting up to a month of abstinence (Hirvonen et al., 2012) (p. 6).

comparison.controls: Not applicable at review level. Comparators in the cited estimates: people who had not used cannabis or had not tried it by 18 (psychosis, depression); people who never used and people who used but not persistently (Dunedin); drivers without cannabis, and non-culpable drivers (crashes); people who had stopped using and people who never used (injury admissions); co-twins who did not use (school leaving, other drugs); community and age-matched controls (suicide attempts, cancers).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review notes that people who use cannabis regularly may differ at baseline in their risks (other drug use, risk-taking) (p. 4), that the least cognitively able young people are the most likely to start early and use regularly (p. 6), and that genetic differences in IQ and in conduct and substance use disorders could explain findings in children exposed before birth (p. 4). For psychosis it calls the common-cause hypothesis harder to exclude (p. 8) but does not discuss shared genetic liability or genetically informed tests.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (no data). Outcomes named: crash risk and culpability; birthweight, birth defects and child development; DSM-III dependence (1993 review) and later cannabis abuse and dependence (instrument not named); withdrawal; treatment entry; IQ change, cognitive deficits (tests not named) and event-related potentials; PET CB1 receptor binding, functional and structural MRI; school completion; other illicit drug use; schizophrenia diagnosis, psychotic symptoms or disorders, age at first episode; depression, mania, suicide attempts, ideation, self-harm and suicide deaths; bronchitis symptoms, lung function and emphysema; myocardial infarction and mortality after infarction; lung, head and neck, prostate, testicular and childhood cancers.
outcomes.operationalization: A conclusion is drawn when the evidence makes it more likely than not that cannabis is a cause (p. 2). Table 1 rates each outcome with symbols (+++, ++, +?) that the paper does not define, a level of evidence and a strength of effect (for example a twofold effect in regular use, '3–4-fold for MI', 'Difficult to quantify') (p. 12).

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed; all cited (sources in the key findings). Crashes: pooled OR 1.92 (95% CI 1.35–2.73), subgroups 2.21 vs 1.78, 2.79 vs 1.65 and 2.10 vs 1.74; a second meta-analysis 2.66; 2–3 times against 6–15 times for alcohol; 2.5% of French traffic deaths against 29% for alcohol (no citation). Dependence: 9% of people who had ever used (US, early 1990s) against 32% nicotine, 23% heroin, 17% cocaine, 15% alcohol and 11% stimulants; one in six who start in adolescence; half of people who use daily; 1–2% of adults in the past year and 4–8% in their lifetime. Cognition: an 8-point IQ decline with early-onset persistent use (Dunedin, n=1037). Psychosis: 2.4 and 2.3 times (Swedish conscripts); 13% of cases avertable; pooled OR 1.4 (1.20–1.65) for ever use and 2.09 (1.54–2.84) for the regular-use category; the author's absolute estimate of 7 rising to 14 in 1000; 4700 young men to be dissuaded per case prevented; 10% rising to 20% for people with an affected first-degree relative under a multiplicative model. Depression: 1.5 times (not significant after adjustment); pooled OR 1.49 (1.15–1.94). Suicide: adjusted OR 2 (case–control); OR 5.3 (3.3–7.79) and 4.8 (2.4–8.9) in a treatment cohort. Myocardial infarction: risk quadrupled in the hour after use. Cancers: head and neck OR 2; lung OR 8.2 (no citation) and a doubling at 50 or more uses by 18; no overall cancer excess, RR 0.9 (0.7–1.2); testicular germ cell tumour OR 1.7 (1.1–2.5), non-seminoma 2.3 (1.4–4.0). School leaving: early use contributing 17% of the risk of not completing school or post-secondary training. Editors' calculations: the implied absolute difference in the psychosis estimate is 7 per 1000; the suicide case–control percentages (16% against 2%) give a crude odds ratio of about 9 before adjustment.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable; adjustment sets are given for a few cited estimates only (Swedish 2.3: personal psychiatric history by 18 and parental divorce; Dunedin: recent cannabis use, alcohol, tobacco and other drug use, schizophrenia symptoms and, in a subgroup, education; school leaving: parental social class and other measures of disadvantage; suicide case–control: social disadvantage, depression and alcohol dependence; head and neck cancer: cigarettes, alcohol and other risk factors).
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. A published critique of the Dunedin IQ analysis that argues for confounding by socioeconomic status (Rogeberg, 2013, PNAS; on the project's list) is not cited, although it appeared before submission in April 2014. The body reports counter-evidence (discordant twins for school leaving; attenuation with adjustment for psychosis; null and mixed findings for respiratory function, cancers, depression and suicide) that the abstract and conclusions summarize more favourably to a causal reading.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In the body, second-hand: crash risk about doubled (OR 1.92); dependence in about 9% of everyone who had ever used cannabis and in about half of people who use daily, in one prospective study; an 8-point IQ decline confined to the small group with adolescent-onset, persistent near-daily use in one cohort, with some recovery after a year without use; pooled odds ratios of 1.4 (ever use) and 2.09 (regular-use category) for psychotic symptoms or disorders that attenuate with adjustment, a common-cause hypothesis the author calls harder to exclude and mixed evidence on incidence trends; school-leaving associations that persisted after adjustment in cohorts but were absent within discordant twin pairs; mixed or confounded evidence on depression, suicide, lung function and respiratory cancers; a probable acute risk of myocardial infarction in middle-aged adults.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Abstract (p. 1): regular adolescent use "approximately doubles the risks of early school-leaving and of cognitive impairment and psychoses in adulthood"; the associations persist after controlling for plausible confounders in longitudinal studies, which suggests that cannabis is a contributory cause; and about one in ten people who use cannabis regularly develop dependence. Conclusions (p. 12): adolescent-onset regular use "appears to produce cognitive impairment", and "All these relationships have persisted after controlling for plausible confounders in well-designed studies". Gaps: (1) no doubling of cognitive impairment is reported in the body, and Table 1 calls the effect difficult to quantify; (2) no doubling of early school-leaving is reported, and the body's discordant-twin evidence points to shared genetic and environmental risk factors (pp. 6–7), so the education association did not survive the review's own strongest test; (3) for psychosis the body says the association attenuated with adjustment and that no study assessed all confounders (p. 8), which the conclusions' wording does not convey, and no genetically informed test is cited; (4) the 1-in-10 dependence figure in the body refers to everyone who had ever used, not to regular use (p. 5); (5) the Dunedin finding is presented without its published critique. The review does state its more-likely-than-not standard of proof, which accounts for some of its causal wording, and it labels its potency statements as hypotheses.

timeline.event: Swedish conscript cohort (Andréasson et al., 1987, as described here): the one large prospective study in the 1993 review supporting a causal role; critics (not named) argued it had not addressed confounding and reverse causation.
The author's review for the Australian government (Hall, Solowij & Lemon, 1994, ref 9), the 1993 baseline against which this paper compares the 2013 evidence.
US National Comorbidity Survey analysis cited for the lifetime dependence risks of other drugs (32% nicotine, 23% heroin, 17% cocaine, 15% alcohol, 11% stimulants).

Full recovery after 28 days of abstinence (Pope et al., 2001), set against persistent dose-related impairment after 28 days (Bolla et al., 2002): the conflicting cognitive-recovery findings the review places side by side.

27-year follow-up of the Swedish cohort (Zammit et al., 2002): dose–response persisting after adjustment; 13% of schizophrenia cases avertable. Supporting cohorts: the Netherlands (van Os et al., 2002), Germany (Henquet et al., 2004), New Zealand (Arseneault et al., 2002; Fergusson et al., 2003).

Tests of the shared-risk explanation for other illicit drug use: discordant twins (Lynskey et al., 2003; similar US and Dutch twin results), fixed-effects regression (Fergusson et al., 2006) and a simulation showing shared risk factors could explain the US associations (Morral et al., 2002); associations persisted in the first two.

Incidence-trend test by the author's group (Degenhardt, Hall & Lynskey, 2003): no rise in psychosis incidence in Australia after steep rises in use; also cited: too early to detect in Britain (Hickman et al., 2007), rises in recent birth cohorts in south-east London (Boydell et al., 2006) and Zurich (Ajdacic-Gross et al., 2007), no rise in a British general-practice study (cited via the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs, 2008).

Systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal studies: pooled OR 1.4 (ever use) and 2.09 (regular-use category) for psychotic outcomes, 1.49 for depression; suicide studies too varied to pool (as cited here).
The author's earlier review with Degenhardt: much of the text and many of the figures recur here; it is not cited by this review.
Dunedin birth cohort (Meier et al., 2012): an 8-point IQ decline from 13 to 38 with early-onset persistent use, the central new cognitive evidence in this review.
Meta-analysis of nine case–control and culpability studies of crashes, cited for OR 1.92.
CARDIA cohort of more than 5000 young adults followed for 20 years, cited for lung function and emphysema.

Discordant-twin test of the school-leaving association (Verweij et al., 2013): no difference within twin pairs, which the review reads as shared genetic and environmental risk; supported by two US twin analyses (Grant et al., 2012; Bergen et al., 2008).
40-year lung-cancer follow-up of the Swedish conscripts, cited for a doubling at the heaviest exposure.

Published critique of the Dunedin IQ analysis arguing that the correlations are consistent with confounding by socioeconomic status (Rogeberg, 2013, PNAS), and the cohort authors' reply (Moffitt et al., 2013); both appeared before this review was submitted and neither is cited (titles from the project's list).
After this review: re-analysis of the crash meta-analyses it cites (Asbridge et al., 2012; Li et al., 2012), with lower corrected estimates.

replication.where_it_stands: A narrative review that largely restates and extends Hall & Degenhardt (2009) (card sc_hall_2009), so the two count once. Cite it for the author's 2013 judgments (as his), its causal criteria and standard of proof, and as a pointer to primary studies; take the numbers from the primaries (dependence: card sc_anthony_1994 and, not cited here, card sc_lopez_quintero_2011 for cumulative transition probabilities; psychosis and depression pooling: card sc_moore_2007; crashes: card sc_asbridge_2012, re-analysed in card sc_rogeberg_2016; lung function: card sc_pletcher_2012; lung cancer: card sc_callaghan_2013). The Dunedin IQ finding was disputed before this review appeared (Rogeberg, 2013; reply by Moffitt et al., 2013), and later twin studies of cognition (Jackson et al., 2016; Meier et al., 2018) and later reviews of the psychosis evidence (Gage et al., 2016; Gillespie & Kendler, 2021, whose title names genetically informed methods) are on the project's list; none is discussed here.

funding.funder: NHMRC Australia Fellowship 569738, stated as funding for research on this paper (Funding, p. 12).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Queensland Centre for Youth Substance Abuse Research and UQ Centre for Clinical Research, Herston; National Addiction Centre, King's College London; National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales (p. 1). The paper was presented at a drug-policy symposium (Auckland, November 2013). The author led the 1993 review that frames this one; the acknowledgements thank Nadia Solowij and Jim Lemon (1994 review), Louisa Degenhardt, Michael Lynskey, Bianca Calabria (help for a Global Burden of Disease project), Jason Connor (comments on a draft) and Sarah Yeates (literature searches) (pp. 12–13). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: For the causal questions the review leaves open (psychosis, cognition, school leaving): designs that remove shared liability (co-twin and sibling comparisons; genetically informed methods with valid instruments) and prospective cohorts that test cognition before first use and again after sustained abstinence, with frequency and THC content measured; for dependence, prospective estimates of transition by frequency and potency with a stated denominator.

domains.note: No search method, sources, dates or criteria; the abstract's Methods is a comparison with the author's 1993 review; literature searches are mentioned only in the acknowledgements.

No formal appraisal. Limits are named for some studies (under-reported use in pregnancy; tobacco confounding in cancer studies; register data in the Norwegian suicide cohort; little regular use and follow-up only to age 42 in the Kaiser cohort), but the Dunedin IQ study is presented without its critique and pooled estimates without heterogeneity, exposure definitions or adjustment sets.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The frame is the author's own 1993 review; 13 of 165 references are his (31 of 225 citation instances, editors' count), his 2010 book is the most-cited source, and the null Australian incidence-trend test is his group's. The main psychosis, cognition and crash evidence is by others.

The standard of proof is stated and the potency statements are labelled plausible hypotheses; but the abstract states a doubling of cognitive impairment and of early school-leaving that the body does not show, Table 1 gives strengths of effect with no source in the text (chronic bronchitis, educational outcomes, suicide), and several figures carry no citation.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a causal reading
domains.note: The body gives sceptics' arguments, attenuation with adjustment, mixed incidence trends and the null discordant-twin result for school leaving; the abstract and conclusions under-represent them, and the published socioeconomic-confounding critique of the Dunedin IQ finding (Rogeberg, 2013) is not mentioned. Benefits are outside the scope by design.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument exists for narrative reviews (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used and the overall judgment follows the worst domain. There is no search method, every figure is second-hand, and the abstract and Table 1 state effects more strongly than the body. Cite the review for the author's 2013 judgments, labelled as his, for its causal criteria and standard of proof, and as a pointer to the primary studies named in the key findings; take numbers from the primaries. It overlaps Hall & Degenhardt (2009) heavily, so the two are not independent support. A claim resting only on this review stays at draft and must say its figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3).

key_findings.finding: Approach, restated from the 1993 review and applied to 2013: evidence of (i) an association in case–control and prospective studies, (ii) reverse causation being implausible (for example use preceding the outcome), (iii) prospective control of confounders such as other drug use, and (iv) clinical and experimental support for biological plausibility; a standard of proof of "more likely than not" rather than beyond reasonable doubt; inference also allowed where cannabis shares a route with tobacco smoking (respiratory disease), acute effects with alcohol (driving) or pharmacology with long-acting CNS depressants; and the same evidential standards as for alcohol and tobacco. The abstract's Methods is a comparison of the 1993 evidence with that of 2013; no search is described.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Methods); OUR APPROACH TO THE LITERATURE IN 1993, 3rd–7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Definitions and the main problem of interpretation: heavy or regular use is usually defined as daily or near-daily use, a pattern that over years and decades predicts many adverse effects (Hall & Pacula, 2010, the author's book); unless stated otherwise the review concerns regular, typically daily, smoking. Epidemiological studies usually cannot measure THC or CBD doses. People who use cannabis regularly differ at baseline (more alcohol, tobacco and other illicit drug use; risk-taking); statistical adjustment and fixed-effects regression (for example Fergusson et al., 2005) have been used to test confounding, and doubts have been expressed about the former (Macleod et al., 2004).
key_findings.locator: WHY ARE WE CONCERNED ABOUT RECREATIONAL CANNABIS USE?, 4th paragraph (p. 2); ADVERSE HEALTH EFFECTS OF CHRONIC CANNABIS USE, 1st–2nd paragraphs (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Potency: US THC content rose from under 2% in 1980 to 8.5% in 2006 (ElSohly, 2008 report) and also rose in the Netherlands and probably other developed countries (McLaren et al., 2008). In 1993 there were claims of a sharp rise, and US seizure analyses reported a 30% increase, but there were no good trend data outside the USA as late as 1999 (Hall & Swift, 2000); since 2000 it is clearer that THC content rose in the 1990s and early 2000s, and less clear whether CBD fell. The author lists as plausible hypotheses that higher THC may increase anxiety, depression and psychotic symptoms in people new to cannabis (perhaps explaining more emergency attendances) and the risks of dependence and psychotic symptoms in people who use regularly; he cites evidence that people who use regularly compensate only partly for more potent products (van der Pol et al., 2014). That study, whose title concerns dependence, is the only potency study cited and is cited for dose adjustment only; no study of potency and psychosis is cited.
key_findings.locator: WHY ARE WE CONCERNED ABOUT RECREATIONAL CANNABIS USE?, 2nd paragraph (p. 1); THE HEALTH EFFECTS OF INCREASED THC IN CANNABIS PRODUCTS, 1st–3rd paragraphs (p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Acute effects: no fatal overdoses are reported in the epidemiological literature (Calabria et al., 2010, co-authored by the author); the estimated fatal human dose, derived from animal studies, is 15 g (Gable, 2004) to 70 g (Iversen, 2007), far more than a person who uses very heavily could use in a day; case reports describe cardiovascular deaths in seemingly healthy young men after smoking cannabis (Hartung et al., 2014). Anxiety, panic reactions and psychotic symptoms continue to be reported, especially by people new to cannabis, and US emergency attendances in which cannabis is mentioned rose over the past decade (SAMHSA, 2013; no figures given). Table 1 rates fatal overdose as +++ (no case reports; strength of effect 0).
key_findings.locator: ADVERSE ACUTE HEALTH EFFECTS, 1st–3rd paragraphs (pp. 2–3); Table 1, Fatal overdose row (p. 12)

key_findings.finding: Crashes: among 64 657 health-maintenance-organisation patients, those who used cannabis had more hospital admissions for injury than those who had stopped or never used, with motor-vehicle accident RR 1.96 persisting after adjustment in men (Gerberich et al., 2003); a similar relation in 900 drivers hospitalized with injuries and 900 age- and sex-matched non-trauma controls (Mura et al., 2003). A meta-analysis of nine case–control and culpability studies (Asbridge et al., 2012) found that recent use (THC in blood or self-report) roughly doubled crash risk, OR 1.92 (95% CI 1.35–2.73), described as marginally higher in better-designed studies (2.21 vs 1.78), case–control rather than culpability studies (2.79 vs 1.65) and fatalities rather than injuries (2.10 vs 1.74); another meta-analysis pooled 2.66 (Li et al., 2012). Summary: crash risk 2–3 times when driving intoxicated (Ramaekers et al., 2004) against 6–15 times for comparable intoxicating doses of alcohol; cannabis estimated to account for 2.5% of traffic deaths in France against 29% for alcohol (no citation); risk rises substantially with alcohol as well (Hartman & Huestis, 2013).
key_findings.locator: ADVERSE ACUTE HEALTH EFFECTS › Car crash injuries and deaths, 3rd–5th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The pooled and subgroup figures match card sc_asbridge_2012, which records the non-fatal subgroup interval as 0.88–3.46 (including 1); 'marginally higher' understates the 2.79 against 1.65 split. Both meta-analyses were later re-analysed with lower corrected estimates (card sc_rogeberg_2016). The French figure is cited in Hall & Degenhardt (2009, p. 1385) to Laumon et al. (2005).

key_findings.finding: Pregnancy and children: birth defects not consistently increased, with the most convincing null result in a large sample whose use was measured by urinalysis (Zuckerman et al., 1989). A meta-analysis of 1980s and 1990s studies suggested that regular use in pregnancy reduced birthweight, less than tobacco (English et al., 1997); later large studies reported that use in pregnancy is associated with reduced birthweight (for example Hayatbakhsh et al., 2012; Fergusson et al., 2002), an effect that has generally persisted after statistical control for other drug use (cited to Zuckerman et al., 1989; Fergusson et al., 2002; El Marroun et al., 2009), and several of these studies reported shorter labour and more small-for-gestational-age babies (Hayatbakhsh et al., 2012). Self-reported use in pregnancy is typically low (2–6%, no citation); urinalysis studies suggest considerable under-reporting, which probably attenuates the associations with poor birth outcomes, and it has often been difficult to adjust fully for cigarette smoking (p. 4). Children: no full-scale IQ difference at 12 but differences in perceptual organization and higher cognitive processes in the Ontario study (Fried & Smith, 2001); no IQ difference at 1 year in 756 women, a third of whom used cannabis (Tennes et al., 1985); in the Pittsburgh cohort of 655 low-income women, lower memory and verbal scores at 3 (Day et al., 1994), delinquency and problem behaviour at 10 (Goldschmidt et al., 2000), poorer reading and spelling (Goldschmidt et al., 2004) and poorer school performance at 14 mediated by lower cognitive ability, attention and mood disorders and cannabis use before 14 (Goldschmidt et al., 2012). Behavioural effects are reported in only two cohorts, and genetic differences between mothers were not controlled (Huizink & Mulder, 2006).
key_findings.locator: Reproductive effects of cannabis use › Fetal development and birth defects, 1st–3rd paragraphs; Postnatal effects of maternal cannabis use, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Dependence: the 1993 review used the DSM-III definition (impaired control over use, difficulty stopping despite harm). Cannabis abuse and dependence remain the most common drug dependence after alcohol and tobacco in Australian, Canadian and US surveys, affecting an estimated 1–2% of adults in the past year and 4–8% in their lifetime (Hall & Pacula, 2010; Anthony, 2006). The lifetime risk of dependence among people who have ever used cannabis was estimated at 9% in the USA in the early 1990s (Anthony, 2006, a book chapter), against 32% for nicotine, 23% for heroin, 17% for cocaine, 15% for alcohol and 11% for stimulants (Anthony et al., 1994; Hall et al., 1999). In longitudinal studies, the risk was estimated at one in six among those who started in adolescence (Anthony, 2006) and half of people who use daily (van der Pol et al., 2013).
key_findings.locator: ADVERSE HEALTH EFFECTS OF CHRONIC CANNABIS USE › Cannabis dependence, 1st paragraph (p. 4, continued on p. 5) and 2nd paragraph (p. 5)
key_findings.note: Second-hand; repeated from Hall & Degenhardt (2009, p. 1386). The 9% and the comparison figures match the 1990–92 National Comorbidity Survey proportions of people who had ever used each drug who had ever met DSM-III-R dependence (card sc_anthony_1994: cannabis 9.1%, tobacco 31.9%, heroin 23.1%, cocaine 16.7%, alcohol 15.4%, other stimulants 11.2%), from a cross-sectional survey; Hall et al. (1999, ref 41) is, by its title, a 12-month prevalence survey of Australian adults. 'One in six' is cited only to a book chapter; 'half of people who use daily' to a three-year prospective study whose title refers to frequent use, with no definition or follow-up window given here. NESARC cumulative transition probabilities (card sc_lopez_quintero_2011) are not cited. Curran et al. (2016, p. 301) cite the same three-year study (van der Pol et al., 2013) for a different finding: measures of cannabis use did not predict transition to dependence (card sc_curran_2016).

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal and treatment: tolerance to THC develops in laboratory studies (Lichtman & Martin, 2005); the most common withdrawal symptoms are anxiety, insomnia, appetite disturbance and depression (Budney & Hughes, 2006), often severe enough to impair everyday functioning (Allsop et al., 2012); a double-blind trial found withdrawal markedly attenuated by an oral cannabis extract (Sativex; Allsop et al., 2014, whose title names nabiximols). Help-seeking increased in the USA, Europe and Australia, usually about a decade after increases in use among young adults (Roxburgh et al., 2010), and also in the Netherlands, which the author takes as evidence against a court-diversion explanation (EMCDDA, 2013). In 2011 cannabis was the primary drug problem for 48% of people entering drug treatment and for 58% of new treatment entrants in the Netherlands (sentence without citation). Consequences reported by people seeking treatment are less severe than for alcohol or opioid dependence (Hall & Pacula, 2010; Degenhardt & Hall, 2012), recovery rates are similar to alcohol (Flórez-Salamanca et al., 2013), and after cognitive–behaviour therapy only a minority remain abstinent at 6 and 12 months, though most reduce problems and frequency (Roffman & Stephens, 2006; Danovitch & Gorelick, 2012).
key_findings.locator: Cannabis dependence, 3rd–5th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The review calls Sativex an oral cannabis extract; nabiximols is a spray given in the mouth (given sublingually, Huestis, 2007, 2.1.3; an oromucosal spray, card sc_whiting_2015), not a swallowed extract. The sentence ranking the symptoms (most common) is general, not limited to people seeking help.

key_findings.finding: Cognition, 1993 and since: in 1993 case–control studies showed poorer performance in people who used regularly, of unclear direction; very few studies had matched on estimated pre-use intellectual function (Solowij, 2002, chapter) and only one had measured cognition before use (Block et al., 2002); both found greater impairment in frequent or long-term use after controlling for baseline ability. Since 1993 better-controlled studies (reviewed by Crane et al., 2013; Solowij & Battisti, 2008) have consistently found deficits in verbal learning, memory and attention in regular use, usually but not always related to duration and frequency of use, age of initiation and estimated cumulative THC dose (Solowij et al., 2002; Solowij & Pesa, 2012).
key_findings.locator: Chronic cannabis use and cognitive and brain function › Cognitive impairment, 1st–2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Tests, abstinence periods and effect sizes are not given; see reporting issues on the dates of the two pre-use studies.

key_findings.finding: Recovery of cognition: it remains unclear whether function recovers fully after stopping long-term use; partial recovery after 2 years of abstinence, with event-related potentials still showing impaired information processing correlated with years of use (Solowij, 2002; Solowij & Pesa, 2012); persistent dose-related impairment after 28 days of abstinence in young people who used heavily, on average for 5 years (Bolla et al., 2002); full recovery after 28 days of abstinence (Pope et al., 2001). Whether any impairment reflects residual effects or more enduring changes from cumulative THC is also unclear (Solowij et al., 2002).
key_findings.locator: Cognitive impairment, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Hall & Degenhardt (2009, p. 1387) reported Bolla et al. as 'indications of' persistent impairment and Pope et al. as recovery; the wording here is firmer in both directions.

key_findings.finding: Dunedin birth cohort (Meier et al., 2012): IQ was tested at 13 (before cannabis use) and at 38 in 1037 people born in 1972 or 1973; early and persistent use went with an average IQ decline of 8 points compared with people who never used and people who used but not persistently. The decline was largest with adolescent onset and continued near-daily use through adulthood; it persisted after adjustment for recent cannabis use, alcohol, tobacco and other drug use and schizophrenia symptoms, and among those who finished high school after controlling for education; there was some recovery after a year or more without use, and no decline in people who started as adults and had not used for a year or more before follow-up. The effects were found only in the small proportion who started in adolescence and used daily through their 20s and into their 30s; informants rated them as having more memory and attention problems in everyday life.
key_findings.locator: Cognitive impairment, 3rd–5th paragraphs (from p. 5)
key_findings.note: One cohort; the review gives neither the number in the persistent-use group nor any adjustment for socioeconomic status, and it does not mention the published critique (Rogeberg, 2013). See reporting issues on the review's restatement of the 8 points.

key_findings.finding: Brain structure and function: the 1993 review found a 22-year-old air-encephalography study suggesting structural damage, since heavily criticized (small sample, poor control of other drug use, doubtful method) (Campbell et al., 1971). PET showed down-regulation of cannabinoid receptors in people who use cannabis regularly that persisted for up to a month of abstinence (Hirvonen et al., 2012, whose title calls it reversible); functional imaging showed reduced activity in memory and attention regions after 28 days of abstinence (for example Quickfall & Crockford, 2006; Block et al., 2002); MRI showed smaller hippocampal and amygdala volumes in 15 people who had smoked five or more joints a day for 10 or more years, largest with the longest use (Yücel et al., 2008). Reviews call for larger, better-controlled studies with standardized tasks (Baker et al., 2013; Batalla et al., 2013). The author adds that the least cognitively able young people are the most likely to start early and use regularly.
key_findings.locator: Brain structure and function, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: School leaving: use before 15 was related to early school-leaving after adjustment for confounders (for example Ellickson et al., 1998); in three Australian and New Zealand longitudinal studies (Horwood et al., 2010, described as a meta-analysis) the earlier the first use, the lower the chances of completing school and post-secondary training, after adjustment for parental social class and other measures of disadvantage, and early use was estimated to contribute 17% of the risk of not completing. In Australian twins discordant for early use there was no difference in early school-leaving between the twin who used and the twin who did not (Verweij et al., 2013), suggesting shared genetic and environmental risk factors, supported by two earlier US twin analyses (Grant et al., 2012; Bergen et al., 2008).
key_findings.locator: The psychosocial consequences of adolescent cannabis use › Educational outcomes, 2nd and 4th paragraphs (the 4th continued on p. 7)
key_findings.note: School leaving is the only genetically informed (discordant-twin) test in the review that went against the causal reading: the Other drug use section (p. 7) reports discordant-twin studies (Lynskey et al., 2003, and US and Dutch studies, both cited to ref 86) in which the association with other illicit drug use persisted within pairs; the abstract nevertheless says regular adolescent use approximately doubles the risk of early school-leaving.

key_findings.finding: Other illicit drugs: associations with later heroin and cocaine use persist after statistical adjustment (for example Lessem et al., 2006) and after fixed-effects regression for unmeasured fixed confounders (Fergusson et al., 2006); within twin pairs discordant for cannabis use, the twin who used was more likely to use other illicit drugs after controlling for non-shared environmental factors (Lynskey et al., 2003), with similar US and Dutch results; a simulation indicated that shared risk factors could explain the US associations (Morral et al., 2002). In a 'reverse gateway', people who start with cannabis are now more likely to start smoking tobacco (Patton et al., 2005), more strongly in an Australian study, where tobacco is commonly mixed into joints, than in a US study (Timberlake et al., 2007).
key_findings.locator: Other drug use, 2nd–6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Psychosis, Swedish conscripts: in 1993 the one large prospective study supporting a causal role was a 15-year follow-up of 50 465 male conscripts: those who had tried cannabis by 18 were 2.4 times more likely to be diagnosed with schizophrenia over the next 15 years, and after adjustment for a personal history of psychiatric disorder by 18 and parental divorce, those who had used ten or more times by 18 were 2.3 times more likely (Andréasson et al., 1987). Critics, not named or cited, argued the study had not addressed confounding and reverse causation.
key_findings.locator: Cannabis use and mental health › Psychosis and schizophrenia, 2nd–3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Exposure: self-reported use by 18; outcome: schizophrenia diagnosis; comparator: men who had not used. Second-hand; take the estimates from the primary (Andréasson et al., 1987).

key_findings.finding: Psychosis, later cohorts: the 27-year follow-up of the Swedish cohort found a dose–response between frequency of use at 18 and schizophrenia over the whole follow-up, persisting after adjustment, and estimated that 13% of cases could have been averted if all cannabis use had been prevented (Zammit et al., 2002). Smaller longitudinal studies in the Netherlands (van Os et al., 2002), Germany (Henquet et al., 2004) and New Zealand (Arseneault et al., 2002; Fergusson et al., 2003) found associations with psychotic disorders or symptoms that persisted after adjustment.
key_findings.locator: Psychosis and schizophrenia, 3rd paragraph (p. 7, continued on p. 8)
key_findings.note: Adjustment sets are not given. The 13% is an attributable fraction that assumes the association is causal.

key_findings.finding: Psychosis, pooled estimates: a meta-analysis of these longitudinal studies (Moore et al., 2007) found psychotic symptoms or psychotic disorders more common in people who had ever used cannabis (pooled OR 1.4, 95% CI 1.20–1.65) and higher in the category the review calls regular use (OR 2.09, 95% CI 1.54–2.84). Reverse causation was addressed in some of the studies by excluding people with psychotic symptoms at baseline or adjusting for them. The common-cause hypothesis was harder to exclude because the association was attenuated by adjustment and no study assessed all confounders.
key_findings.locator: Psychosis and schizophrenia, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: The outcome combines symptoms and disorders; the exposure categories, the studies pooled and their adjustment sets must be taken from Moore et al. (card sc_moore_2007). Hall & Degenhardt (2009, p. 1388) said reverse causation was addressed in most of these studies.

key_findings.finding: Incidence trends: sceptics argue that a causal hypothesis is inconsistent with the absence of any rise in schizophrenia incidence as use rose. The evidence is called mixed: no increased psychosis incidence in an Australian modelling study after steep rises in use in the 1980s and 1990s (Degenhardt, Hall & Lynskey, 2003, the author's group); too early to detect an increase in Britain in a British modelling study (Hickman et al., 2007); increased incidence in recent birth cohorts in case-register studies in Britain (Boydell et al., 2006) and Switzerland (Ajdacic-Gross et al., 2007); no increase in a British study of people treated for schizophrenia in general practice (cited only to the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs, 2008). The author argues that even a causal effect would raise incidence only modestly and that detection is complicated by changing diagnostic criteria and services, poor administrative data and possible falls in incidence from social improvements such as antenatal care.
key_findings.locator: Psychosis and schizophrenia, 5th–6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Absolute risk, the author's "best estimate": the risk of developing a psychosis doubles from about 7 in 1000 in people who do not use cannabis (Saha et al., 2005, a systematic review of the prevalence of schizophrenia) to 14 in 1000 in people who use regularly. If cannabis plays a causal role, preventing uptake in the whole population would do little: about 4700 young men aged 20–24 in the UK would have to be dissuaded from smoking cannabis to prevent one case of schizophrenia (Hickman et al., 2007, as cited). If cannabis and genetic risk act independently and multiplicatively, a doubling would raise the risk of a person with an affected first-degree relative from 10% to 20% with regular use (Gottesman, 1991).
key_findings.locator: Psychosis and schizophrenia, 7th paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)
key_findings.note: The 7 in 1000 is a whole-population prevalence figure (by the cited title, ref 102, p. 16) applied to people who do not use cannabis; the 14 in 1000 is the author's doubling of it with the pooled odds ratio for regular use; the outcome changes from schizophrenia to developing a psychosis. Editors' calculation: the implied absolute difference is 7 per 1000. The 4700 and the 10–20% are conditional on causation (and the latter on a multiplicative model). Trace all three to the primaries before use.

key_findings.finding: Course of psychosis: young people with psychoses or psychotic symptoms who use cannabis have an earlier average age at a first episode (Large et al., 2011; no figure given); those with a first episode who stop using have better outcomes than those who continue, with fewer psychotic symptoms and better social functioning (Mullin et al., 2012; Kuepper et al., 2011).
key_findings.locator: Psychosis and schizophrenia, 8th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Depression and bipolar disorder: in longitudinal studies the association with depression is weaker than with psychosis (Degenhardt et al., 2012, the author's chapter); in the Swedish cohort depression was 1.5 times more common with the heaviest use at 18, not significant after adjustment (Manrique-Garcia et al., 2012); a dose–response with frequency by 16 was not significant after adjustment (Fergusson & Horwood, 1997); a meta-analysis found a modest association (OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.15–1.94) and weak support for causation, as most studies had not controlled confounding or excluded depression leading to cannabis use (Moore et al., 2007); similar conclusions from four Australasian birth cohorts (Horwood et al., 2012). Bipolar disorder: much higher rates of cannabis use disorders in clinical samples; baseline use predicted manic symptoms over 3 years in one longitudinal study (Henquet et al., 2006); continued use goes with more manic episodes in some clinical studies; a contributory causal role is possible but unproven because confounding and reverse causation have not been dealt with.
key_findings.locator: Cannabis use and other mental disorders, 2nd paragraph (p. 8) and 3rd paragraph (p. 9)

key_findings.finding: Suicide: in a New Zealand case–control study of suicide attempts resulting in hospitalization, 16% of 302 people who attempted suicide had a cannabis disorder against 2% of 1028 community controls; adjustment for social disadvantage, depression and alcohol dependence substantially reduced but did not eliminate the association (adjusted OR 2) (Beautrais et al., 1999). Prospective evidence is mixed: a dose–response with frequency by 16 did not persist after adjustment (Fergusson & Horwood, 1997); an econometric analysis of the same cohort found that more than weekly use increased reported suicidal ideation in males only (van Ours et al., 2013); self-harm was associated in females only (Patton et al., 1997); heavy use increased depression but not suicide risk (Rasic et al., 2013); an attempted meta-analysis found designs and measures too varied to quantify risk (Moore et al., 2007). In 6445 people treated for a cannabis use disorder in Norway, suicide risk was raised (OR 5.3, CI 3.3–7.79), and 4.8 (95% CI 2.4–8.9) after excluding people known to inject; the register data allowed little control of confounders and the author suggests suicide risk may be raised before treatment (Arendt et al., 2013).
key_findings.locator: Cannabis use and other mental disorders, 4th–6th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Table 1 rates suicide as +? from cohort studies, with a twofold effect in regular use; the only twofold figure in the text is the adjusted case–control odds ratio. Editors' calculation from the rounded percentages: crude odds ratio about 9 before adjustment. The first treatment-cohort interval is printed without its level; take the setting and estimates from the primary.

key_findings.finding: Respiratory effects: people who smoke cannabis regularly report more symptoms of chronic bronchitis (wheeze, sputum, chronic cough) (Tetrault et al., 2007); since 1993 the picture has stayed unclear because most people who smoke cannabis also smoke or have smoked tobacco (Owen et al., 2013). People in a health-maintenance-organisation cohort who smoked only cannabis used more health services for respiratory infections (Tashkin et al., 2002); impaired function in dependent members of a New Zealand cohort of 1037 followed to 26 (Taylor et al., 2002) was not replicated in a larger, longer US follow-up (Tashkin et al., 2002); no increase in emphysema in US (Pletcher et al., 2012; Tashkin, 2005) and New Zealand (Aldington et al., 2007) follow-ups. In CARDIA, more than 5000 young adults over 20 years (Pletcher et al., 2012), tobacco showed a dose–response with poorer function, whereas low levels of cannabis smoking (a median of three to five joints a month) appeared to increase function and function declined in people who smoked cannabis daily; the study's authors suggested frequency-dependent effects.
key_findings.locator: Adverse health effects of long-term cannabis smoking › Respiratory system, 1st–3rd paragraphs (right column)
key_findings.note: Card sc_pletcher_2012 records a different picture of the same study; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular effects: laboratory studies in 1993 showed dose-related rises in heart rate with rapid tolerance in healthy young adults (Jones, 2002; Sidney, 2002) and angina provoked in older adults with cardiovascular disease (Gottschalk et al., 1977). In a case-crossover study of 3882 people who had had a myocardial infarction, cannabis use 'quadrupled' the risk in the hour after smoking (Mittleman et al., 2001); in 1913 of them, frequency of use showed a dose–response with mortality over 3.8 years (Mukamal et al., 2008). A French series of 200 cannabis-related hospitalizations in the Toulouse area (January 2004 to December 2007) included several myocardial infarctions and a fatal stroke in young adults with recent use and no other known risk factors (Jouanjus et al., 2011), from which the author infers that cannabis smoking can provoke fatal cardiovascular events in young people with undiagnosed disease. Table 1: cardiovascular disease ++, from cohort and case–control studies, 3–4-fold for MI.
key_findings.locator: Cardiovascular effects, 1st paragraph (p. 9, continued on p. 10), 2nd–3rd paragraphs (p. 10); Table 1 (p. 12)
key_findings.note: The causal inference for young adults rests on case reports. Hall & Degenhardt (2009, p. 1387) gave the case-crossover estimate as 4.8 times.

key_findings.finding: Respiratory cancers: THC is not carcinogenic in microbial assays or rodents, but cannabis smoke is carcinogenic in laboratory assays. No increase in respiratory cancer over 8.6 years among 64 855 Kaiser Permanente members, though rates of regular use were low and follow-up stopped at 42 (Sidney et al., 1997); head and neck squamous cell carcinoma OR 2 in 173 cases and 176 controls after adjustment for cigarettes, alcohol and other factors (Zhang et al., 1999), against three null case–control studies (Hashibe et al., 2005). Lung cancer: all case–control studies confounded by cigarette smoking (Mehra et al., 2006); a Tunisian study of 110 hospital cases and 110 community controls, OR 8.2 after adjustment for cigarettes (no citation); a pooled analysis of three Moroccan studies in which all who used cannabis also smoked tobacco (Berthiller et al., 2008); a dose–response in 79 cases under 55 and 324 controls in New Zealand (Aldington et al., 2008); US associations not significant after tobacco adjustment (Hashibe et al., 2006); in the 40-year follow-up of the Swedish conscripts, a doubling of lung-cancer risk with 50 or more uses by 18, surviving adjustment for cigarettes, although 91% of the heaviest group also smoked tobacco (Callaghan et al., 2013).
key_findings.locator: Cannabis and cancer, 1st paragraph; Respiratory cancers, 2nd–4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Card sc_callaghan_2013 records the band as more than 50 lifetime uses reported at conscription (age 18 to 20), a fully adjusted HR of 2.12 (95% CI 1.08–4.14) and no clear dose–response across lower bands.

key_findings.finding: Other cancers: three case–control studies found associations between maternal cannabis use and childhood cancers, judged unlikely to be causal in 1993, not replicated since, with no rise in incidence in the USA in 1979–95. Prostate cancer was raised in men who smoked cannabis in the Kaiser cohort, with no overall cancer excess (RR 0.9, 95% CI 0.7–1.2) and possible confounding by lifestyle (Sidney et al., 1997). Testicular germ cell tumours: 369 cases and 979 age-matched controls, OR 1.7 (95% CI 1.1–2.5), non-seminoma OR 2.3 (1.4–4.0), higher with use before 18 and more than weekly use (Daling et al., 2009), replicated in two US case–control studies with a doubling of non-seminoma risk (Lacson et al., 2012; Trabert et al., 2011).
key_findings.locator: Maternal cannabis use and childhood cancers (p. 10, continued on p. 11); Male cancers, 1st–2nd paragraphs (p. 11)

key_findings.finding: What has been learned: the best-designed and most informative studies are two New Zealand birth cohorts, replicated in cohort studies in Australia, Germany and the Netherlands (for example Swift et al., 2008; Wittchen et al., 2007; van Os et al., 2002); that dependence and some adverse effects also occur in the Netherlands, where cannabis has been decriminalized, makes it unlikely that they are due to legal policy. Consistent associations between regular (especially daily) use and adverse health and psychosocial outcomes have often shown dose–response relationships and have persisted after adjustment for plausible confounders.
key_findings.locator: WHAT HAVE WE LEARNED IN 20 YEARS?, 1st–2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Conclusion bullets. Acute: cannabis does not produce fatal overdoses as opioids do; crash risk doubles when driving intoxicated and rises substantially with intoxicating doses of alcohol; maternal use modestly reduces birthweight. Chronic, psychosocial: people who use regularly can develop dependence, at risks of around 1 in 10 of all who use and 1 in 6 among those who start in adolescence; regular use doubles the risk of psychotic symptoms and disorders, especially with a personal or family history of psychotic disorders and initiation in the mid-teens; adolescents who use regularly have lower educational attainment and are more likely to use other illicit drugs; regular use beginning in adolescence and continuing through young adulthood "appears to produce cognitive impairment", with mechanism and reversibility unclear; regular adolescent use approximately doubles the risk of a schizophrenia diagnosis or psychotic symptoms in adulthood; all these relationships persisted after adjustment in well-designed studies, but some researchers question whether they are causal. Physical: higher risks of chronic bronchitis, unclear effect on respiratory function; probably higher risk of myocardial infarction in middle-aged adults.
key_findings.locator: WHAT HAVE WE LEARNED IN 20 YEARS? › Adverse effects of acute use; Adverse effects of chronic use › Psychosocial outcomes; Physical health outcomes (bullet lists)
key_findings.note: The personal or family history and mid-teen initiation qualifiers for psychosis are not supported by evidence in the psychosis section, which raises family history only in a hypothetical multiplicative calculation (p. 8). The qualifier repeats the 1993 review's conclusion, listed among the acute effects (pp. 2–3), of psychotic symptoms at high doses especially with a personal or family history of psychosis; no new evidence for it is presented.

key_findings.finding: Table 1 rates 14 outcomes. Acute: fatal overdose +++, no case reports, 0; road traffic crashes ++, cohort and case–control, 2-fold; low birth weight ++, cohort, no strength given. Chronic: dependence +++, cohort studies, 1 in 10 among people who have ever used; educational outcomes ++, cohort and case–control, 2-fold in regular use; cognitive impairment ++, cohort and case–control, difficult to quantify; psychosis ++, cohort studies, 2-fold in regular use; depression +?, cohort studies, probable confounding; suicide +?, cohort studies, 2-fold in regular use; chronic bronchitis ++, cohort studies, 2-fold in regular use; respiratory impairment +?, cohort studies, mixed; cardiovascular disease ++, cohort and case–control, 3–4-fold for MI. Cancers: testicular ++, case–control, 2–3-fold; respiratory +?, case–control, confounded by smoking. The symbols are not defined anywhere in the paper.
key_findings.locator: Table 1

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says about one in ten people who use cannabis regularly develop dependence; the body gives 9% of everyone who had ever used (p. 5), the conclusions and Table 1 give 1 in 10 of all people who use or have ever used (p. 12), and the body cites about half for daily use (p. 5).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract misstates the denominator; a dependence claim must use the ever-use denominator for the 1-in-10 figure and take any regular-use figure from its primary.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says regular adolescent use approximately doubles the risk of cognitive impairment in adulthood; Table 1 calls the cognitive effect difficult to quantify, and the body reports an 8-point IQ decline in a small subgroup of one cohort, with no relative risk.
reporting_issues.consequence: No doubling of cognitive impairment is supported by the review; do not cite the abstract for it.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says regular adolescent use approximately doubles the risk of early school-leaving, and Table 1 gives a twofold effect in regular use for educational outcomes, but the body reports no twofold estimate (it gives a 17% attributable contribution) and reports that a discordant-twin analysis found no difference within pairs.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure has no source in the review, and the body's strongest test contradicts the causal reading.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's symbols (+++, ++, +?) are not defined; several strengths of effect have no source in the text (a twofold effect in regular use for chronic bronchitis, and for suicide, whose only twofold figure in the text comes from a case–control study while the table names cohort studies and the text calls prospective evidence mixed); dependence is rated from 'Cohort studies' although the 9% comes from a US survey.
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 1 cannot be used as a grading of the evidence or as a source of effect sizes.

reporting_issues.issue: The case-crossover estimate for myocardial infarction is given as a quadrupling of risk in the text (p. 10) and as '3–4-fold for MI' in Table 1 (p. 12); the same study is reported as 4.8 times in Hall & Degenhardt (2009, p. 1387).
reporting_issues.consequence: Three different magnitudes for one study; take the estimate from Mittleman et al. (2001).

reporting_issues.issue: Figures printed without a citation: 2.5% of French traffic deaths against 29% for alcohol (p. 3); self-reported use in pregnancy typically 2–6% (p. 4); 48% of treatment entrants and 58% of new entrants in 2011, with the country of the 48% unclear (p. 5); critics of the Swedish conscript study (p. 7); the Tunisian lung-cancer OR 8.2 (p. 10).
reporting_issues.consequence: These cannot be traced from this review; Hall & Degenhardt (2009) cites Laumon et al. (2005) for the French figure and Berthiller et al. (2008) for the Tunisian study.

reporting_issues.issue: The US and the Dutch discordant-twin studies of other drug use are both cited to ref 86, whose title names a sample of Dutch twins.
reporting_issues.consequence: The US study has no correct citation in the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The Pittsburgh cohort is described as children born to 655 low-income women between 1990 and 1995 and tested at age 3, but the cited paper (ref 31, Day et al.) is dated 1994.
reporting_issues.consequence: The dates cannot be right as printed (also in Hall & Degenhardt, 2009, p. 1386); take them from the primary.

reporting_issues.issue: The paragraph on the 1993 evidence says that very few studies had matched on pre-use intellectual function and only one had measured cognition before use, but cites two 2002 sources for them (Solowij, 2002, a chapter; Block et al., 2002, whose title concerns cerebral blood flow).
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether these were 1993 studies or later ones, which blurs the 1993-against-2013 comparison for cognition; the primary cognitive studies are not named.

reporting_issues.issue: CARDIA (Pletcher et al., 2012) is described as showing that function declined in people who smoked cannabis daily, and is cited for no increase in emphysema. Card sc_pletcher_2012 records cannabis exposure as mostly light (median 2 to 3 episodes in the past 30 days), a negative FEV1 association only at very high exposure that was not statistically significant, too few people with heavy use to confirm harm, and no imaging of emphysema.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's description goes beyond what the primary reports as recorded on that (first-pass) card; cite the primary for lung function, and do not cite it for emphysema.

reporting_issues.issue: The 'best estimate' of 7 rising to 14 in 1000 takes its base rate from a systematic review of the prevalence of schizophrenia (Saha et al., 2005) and applies it to people who do not use cannabis, then doubles it for regular use; the outcome shifts from schizophrenia to developing a psychosis.
reporting_issues.consequence: An illustrative calculation by the author, not a measured risk; an absolute-risk claim must be built from primary incidence data or labelled as the author's estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: The Dunedin 8-point decline is restated as half a standard deviation lower than peers and as an average IQ below 70% of the peer group, which treats a difference in change as a difference in level and is open to misreading as an IQ under 70.
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' calculation, assuming an IQ standard deviation of 15: 8 points is 0.53 SD; a person 0.53 SD below the mean scores below about 70% of a normally distributed reference group, so the sentence means lower than about 70% of peers. Take the magnitude from Meier et al. (2012).

reporting_issues.issue: Reverse causation is said to have been addressed in some of the longitudinal psychosis studies (p. 8); the same author's 2009 review says most (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009, p. 1388).
reporting_issues.consequence: Count the studies that handled reverse causation from Moore et al. (2007), not from either review.

reporting_issues.issue: The Netherlands is said to have decriminalized cannabis use more than 40 years ago (p. 5) and nearly 40 years ago (p. 11).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor internal inconsistency; no bearing on the health claims.

Anchors cite the PDF's own page numbers. No supplementary material is referred to.

disagreements.first_pass: A meta-analysis of 1980s and 1990s studies found regular use in pregnancy reduced birthweight, less than tobacco (English et al., 1997), and later large studies found reduced birthweight persisting after control for other drug use (for example Hayatbakhsh et al., 2012; Fergusson et al., 2002), with shorter labour and more small-for-gestational-age babies; self-reported use in pregnancy is typically low (2–6%, no citation) and under-reported.
disagreements.reviewer: Key finding 5 corrected by second reader 212 (the meta-analysis suggested, not found; add from p. 4 the attenuation by under-reporting and the incomplete adjustment for cigarette smoking); claim writer 210's report: persistence after control is cited to refs 25, 28 and 29, not to Hayatbakhsh et al. (ref 27).
disagreements.resolution: Accepted, both. p. 3 (Fetal development and birth defects, 2nd paragraph): suggested [26]; associated with reduced birth weight [27,28]; persisted after controlling for other drug use [25,28,29]; labour and small for gestational age [27]; p. 4, 3rd paragraph: under-reporting probably attenuates associations, cigarette smoking hard to adjust for. References 25–29 checked on p. 13. Reader 244's claim cl_can_pregnancy_birth (anchor 13) uses the meta-analysis with the verb found: listed for that reader and the editor.

disagreements.first_pass: This is the review's only genetically informed (discordant-twin) test of a causal claim, and it went against the causal reading;
disagreements.reviewer: Key finding 12 corrected by second reader 212: school leaving is not the review's only discordant-twin test; it is the only one that went against the causal reading.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted; p. 7, Other drug use, checked in the PDF text (key finding 13 records the same studies).

disagreements.first_pass: which raises family history only in a hypothetical multiplicative calculation (p. 8).
disagreements.reviewer: Second reader 212, missed item 2: the family-history qualifier repeats a 1993 conclusion listed among the acute effects (pp. 2–3).
disagreements.resolution: Accepted; pp. 2–3 checked in the PDF text.

disagreements.reviewer: Claim writer 209's report and second reader 212 (claim notes): the review calls nabiximols an oral extract, though it is an oromucosal spray; targeted checker 212: the ranking sentence is general.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted; p. 5, Cannabis dependence, 3rd paragraph, checked in the PDF text; the route is taken from two other project sources.

disagreements.first_pass: NESARC cumulative transition probabilities (card sc_lopez_quintero_2011) are not cited.
disagreements.reviewer: Claim writer 209's report: one 3-year study is cited by Hall 2015 and Curran 2016 for different findings.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted as a cross-reference; Curran p. 301 (ref 215) checked in the PDF text.
